vignette:
Marcus

Marcus sits with his hands clasped tightly in his lap, his shoulders drawn up toward his ears in a posture he's held for so long it feels like his natural shape. At fifty-four, he carries himself with the careful deliberation of someone who has learned to take up as little space as possible.

Twenty-three years ago, Marcus was in a relationship with Daniel, a man who initially seemed to share his passion for social justice work. In those early years, Marcus was building his career as a community organizer, working with immigrant populations in his city. He was energized by the work, by the possibility of creating change. But Daniel's love came with conditions that tightened incrementally—criticism about how Marcus dressed, whom he saw, what he said in public. When Marcus tried to establish boundaries, Daniel's hands became the argument. The first time, Marcus convinced himself it was an isolated incident born of stress. By the time the relationship ended, after eighteen months of escalating violence, Marcus had internalized a narrative of complicity that would follow him for decades.

He left Daniel in 1997, but the leaving didn't mean the trauma released its grip. Marcus married his current wife, Sarah, seven years later. On the surface, his life stabilized. He continued his organizing work, became respected in his field, built a life that looked whole to anyone observing from the outside. Yet internally, Marcus remained fractured.

The hypervigilance is his constant companion. When Sarah raises her voice during an argument about household finances, Marcus's body floods with adrenaline. His chest tightens. His mind races through scenarios of escalation he intellectually knows are unlikely but cannot convince his nervous system to dismiss. He finds himself cataloging exits from rooms, noting the weight of objects that could become weapons, tracking Sarah's movements and moods with an exhausting attentiveness that exhausts them both.

Sleep has become a battleground. Marcus lies awake for hours, his mind replaying fragments of memories he thought he'd processed—the sound of Daniel's voice, the feeling of being trapped. When he does sleep, nightmares jolt him awake in cold sweats, sometimes shouting. Sarah has learned not to touch him when he wakes; his startle response is violent and unpredictable, even though the danger exists only in his sleeping mind.

His work, which once felt like purpose, now feels precarious. Last month, during a community meeting, a heated disagreement with a city official triggered something in Marcus. His hands trembled. His voice became thin. He excused himself and sat in his car for forty minutes, breathing deliberately, trying to convince himself that conflict was not violence, that disagreement was not danger. He's begun avoiding certain types of meetings, finding reasons to delegate responsibilities that once energized him. His colleagues have noticed his withdrawal, though they don't know its source.

Marcus carries shame about his trauma in a way that complicates everything. He is a man, and men are supposed to be strong, to protect, not to be protected. He works in social justice, where he helps others name their oppression, yet he has kept his own story largely private, even from Sarah. The secrecy has created a distance between them that neither fully understands. Sarah sees his withdrawal as rejection. Marcus experiences his protective distance as the only way he knows to keep her safe from the damage inside him.

He is here now because Sarah gave him an ultimatum delivered with love: get help or accept that this marriage will slowly suffocate under the weight of his unprocessed past. Marcus chose to come, though hope feels like a luxury he hasn't earned.
